readerTitle: The cleaning company that almost bought a café
caseNote: 가상 사례 (사무실 청소 회사, 물류 회사 사내 소프트웨어 팀) + 실제 연구 (Rumelt 1974, Porter 1987)
insight: 다각화는 위험을 나누는 일이 아니라 지금 가진 능력을 새 사업으로 옮기는 일이다. 무엇이 옮겨 가는지 말할 수 없다면 위험을 줄이는 것이 아니라 늘리는 것이다.
misconception: 달걀을 한 바구니에 담지 말라. 지금 사업과 상관없는 사업을 하나 더 하면 그만큼 안전해진다.

sources.text: Rumelt, R. P. (1974). Strategy, Structure, and Economic Performance. Harvard University Press.
Porter, M. E. (1987). From Competitive Advantage to Corporate Strategy. Harvard Business Review.
청소 회사와 물류 회사 사례는 설명용 가상 사례

factChecks.note: Rumelt(1974): 미국 대기업을 다각화 유형별로 분류해 관련 다각화 기업이 비관련 다각화 기업보다 대체로 성과가 좋았다는 결과. 카드에는 수치 없이 'generally did better'로만 적었습니다. 원문 표현을 확인하세요.
Porter(1987): 1950~1986년 미국 대기업 33곳의 다각화 이력을 조사했고, 새로운 업종에서 인수한 사업의 상당 부분(절반 이상)을 나중에 매각했다는 내용. 카드에는 'sold off many of them'으로 일반화해 적었습니다. 정확한 비율과 표본 수(33곳)를 원문으로 확인하세요.
주주가 스스로 분산 투자하는 편이 더 싸다는 논점은 기업 재무의 표준 논리입니다(예: 다각화 할인 연구 Lang & Stulz 1994, Berger & Ofek 1995). 카드에서는 연구 인용 없이 원리로만 설명했습니다.

cards.title: The cleaning company that almost bought a café
body: Maria runs an office cleaning company with 40 staff. This year two big clients cut their contracts. Half their desks sit empty most days.
Everyone gives her the same advice: don't keep all your eggs in one basket. A friend is selling a busy café. It has nothing to do with offices. That sounds like exactly the point.

image.label: A cleaning van parked outside a café with a for-sale sign
image.brief: 이른 아침 거리. 로고 없는 청소 회사 승합차가 'For sale' 안내문이 붙은 작은 카페 앞에 서 있고, 운전석의 여성 사장이 카페를 바라보며 고민하는 장면. 따뜻한 일러스트, 실제 브랜드나 상표 없음.

cards.title: Which new business should Maria add?
body: Maria wants a second business that doesn't depend on her office clients. She has crews trained in safety and hygiene rules, night-shift scheduling down to a science, and a few vans.
Which move makes the most sense?

options.text: Buy the café. Its ups and downs have nothing to do with offices
options.feedback: The café spreads her income, but Maria knows nothing about food, and none of her strengths carry over. She adds a new risk and splits her attention.

options.text: Launch infection-control cleaning and hygiene checks for medical clinics
options.feedback: New service, new customers, but her trained crews, hygiene know-how and night scheduling all carry over. She starts with an edge instead of from zero.

options.text: Start a moving company, since she already has vans and staff
options.feedback: Vans and people are shared, which helps. But moving needs different skills, insurance and weekend peaks, so the real advantage is thinner than it looks.

cards.title: The café felt safe. It wasn't.
body: The café's income wouldn't rise and fall with offices. That part was true. But Maria would be a beginner competing with owners who had run cafés for years.

The clinic idea was different. Clinics needed cleaning at night, to strict rules, by staff who show up reliably. That was already what her company did best. Her risk wasn't gone, but she would face it with **skills she already had**.

cards.title: Diversification
body: **Diversification** means adding a business with new products for new customers, both at once. It's the boldest of the growth moves, because neither the offer nor the buyer is familiar.

It comes in two kinds. *Related* diversification shares something real with the core: a skill, an asset, a customer relationship. *Unrelated* diversification shares only the owner and the bank account.

image.label: Two paths from one company: one with shared skills, one with nothing shared
image.brief: 가운데 청소 회사 건물. 오른쪽으로 '병원 위생 관리'로 가는 길에는 'Trained crews', 'Hygiene rules', 'Night scheduling' 표지판이 이어져 있고, 왼쪽으로 '카페'로 가는 길에는 표지판 없이 빈 길. 깔끔한 인포그래픽 스타일, 로고 없음.

cards.title: Researchers keep finding the same pattern.
body: In a 1974 study of large US companies, Richard Rumelt found that firms diversifying into related businesses generally did better than those buying into unrelated ones.

In 1987, Michael Porter traced decades of diversification by large US firms. Many had entered new industries, then later **sold off many of those businesses**. The moves that lasted tended to share real skills or activities with the core.
cards.softwareNote: Software teams are tempted to diversify because code feels reusable. The question is the same: does anything beyond general coding skill carry over, such as data, customers or know-how in one industry?

cards.title: Three questions before you diversify.
body: Ask these before any move into a new product for new customers:
list: **What transfers?** Name the specific skill, asset or relationship.
**Would we beat the people already there?** Being new is not an edge.
**Who is the risk really spread for?** Investors can spread their own money more cheaply than a company can.
cards.callout: If you can't answer the first question, you're adding risk, not spreading it.

cards.title: Related doesn't mean safe.
body: Shared skills on paper often turn out smaller in practice. Leaders tend to overestimate how much will carry over and underestimate how much the new business will distract them.

There's a fair side too. A small owner with everything in one business may reasonably want some protection. And when a core market is shrinking for good, staying put can be the riskiest move. Diversify for those reasons, but still go where your strengths travel.

cards.title: Now it's a software team inside a delivery firm.
body: Your in-house team built a route-planning tool that cut fuel costs at your regional delivery company. Leadership wants the team to earn outside revenue. Which new business should it try?

image.label: A small team looking at a map with delivery routes on a screen
image.brief: 사무실의 소규모 개발팀이 큰 화면 속 배송 경로 지도를 함께 보는 장면. 화면에는 선과 점으로 된 경로만, 실제 앱이나 회사 로고 없음.

options.text: Build a consumer fitness app, since apps are a big market
options.feedback: Only general coding skill carries over. The team would face experienced consumer app makers with no data, customers or know-how on its side.

options.text: Sell the route tool to other mid-size delivery firms, with a small support team
options.feedback: The tool, the route data and the team's grasp of delivery work all transfer. The cost is learning to sell and support outside customers, which is a real new skill.

options.text: Offer general IT consulting to any local business
options.feedback: It uses the team's skills and can start quickly. But its real edge is delivery logistics, and here it competes with many consultancies on equal terms.

cards.title: Diversify toward what you're good at, not away from what scares you.
body: A second business protects you only if you can win in it. Choose new markets where a real strength travels with you.
**Try it today:** list three things your business does better than most. Next to each, name one customer group outside your current market that would pay for it.
